name: Becoming a Farmer Trainer: Agricultural Extension and Farmer Business Advisors
objectives: Given the people who support farmers in your area, describe the roles of a lead farmer, a Farmer Business Advisor and an extension agent and who you will link with, naming one local contact or office for each where they exist

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Teaching farmers so it sticks

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Lead farmers, Farmer Business Advisors and extension agents
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe the roles in farmer extension and name who you will link with.
This lesson builds toward: Given the people who support farmers in your area, you will describe the roles of a lead farmer, a Farmer Business Advisor and an extension agent and who you will link with, naming one local contact or office for each where they exist.
Extension means helping farmers learn and use better practices. Government extension agents (in Nigeria, state Agricultural Development Programmes, supported by NAERLS; in Kenya, county agricultural officers working with research bodies such as KALRO) are trained advisers, but each one serves very many farmers. So farmers themselves carry much of the teaching.
A lead farmer or volunteer farmer trainer is a respected farmer who hosts demonstrations and teaches neighbours, usually trained and backed by a project or extension office. In East Africa, ICRAF and partners have used volunteer farmer trainers widely, for example in dairy; an evaluation in Uganda found farmers' knowledge, milk output and income improved.
A Farm Business Advisor (FBA), also called a Farmer Business Advisor, is a local entrepreneur who sells inputs and advice to nearby farmers and earns from commissions and fees. iDE trains FBAs in Zambia and Mozambique, each serving about 80 to 120 farmers. In West and Central Africa, GIZ's Farmer Business School has trained cocoa and food-crop farmers in Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Nigeria and Cameroon in farm business skills, working with extension services. Whatever your title, you complement the extension agent; you do not replace them.
Step by step:
- List who supports farmers in your area: extension office, projects, cooperatives, agrovets.
- Decide which role fits you: lead farmer, FBA, or both.
- Meet your local extension officer and explain what you plan to do.
- Write one contact for each role and when you will next speak.
Words to know:
- Extension: services that help farmers learn and use better practices.
- Lead farmer: a respected farmer who hosts demonstrations and teaches neighbours, often with project or extension support.
- Farm (or Farmer) Business Advisor (FBA): a local entrepreneur who sells inputs and gives advice to nearby farmers for a commission or fee.
Official sources:
- National Agricultural Extension and Research Liaison Services (NAERLS), Nigeria
- Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO)
- CGIAR / ICRAF: Volunteer farmer trainer approach in Eastern Africa
- iDE: Farm Business Advisors
- GIZ: Sustainable Smallholder Agribusiness (Farmer Business School, West and Central Africa)
Try it now: Make a table of who supports farmers in your area: the extension office, any project or cooperative, and the nearest agrovet or input dealer. Write which role you will take (lead farmer, FBA or both) and one contact for each role.
You can now explain the roles in farmer extension and where you fit.

check.q: What mainly makes a Farm Business Advisor different from a volunteer lead farmer?
options: An FBA earns from selling inputs and services
An FBA is a government employee
An FBA only works in towns
check.why: FBAs are local entrepreneurs who earn from commissions and fees.

check.q: You plan to start training neighbours. Who should you meet first?
check.why: Working with extension keeps your advice current and builds support.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: How adults learn, and planning a short session
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a 60 to 90 minute training session that follows show, try, discuss.
This lesson builds toward: Given one practice you know well, you will plan a 60 to 90 minute training session that follows show, try, discuss, with one clear skill, timings, materials and a check that every farmer can do it.
Adult farmers learn best by doing, from people they trust, about problems they have now. They bring experience: respect it and ask what they already do. Long talks are forgotten; doing it with their own hands is remembered. Use three steps: show (you demonstrate the skill slowly, explaining why), try (every farmer does it while you watch and help), discuss (the group talks about what they saw, what is hard, and whether it will work on their farms).
Teach one skill per session, such as "measure and plant maize in rows with one handful of compost per hole", not "everything about maize". Plan it: the skill; materials for everyone to try; timings (for example 10 minutes welcome and what you do now, 15 show, 30 try, 20 discuss, 10 plan and check); and how you will check that each farmer can do it, such as watching each one plant three holes correctly.
Pick a time that suits farmers (after morning work, not on market day), a place they can reach, and a language they speak. Include women and young people: ask who does the work at home and invite them. Keep groups small enough for everyone to try, about 15 to 25 people per trainer.
Step by step:
- Choose one skill the farmers need now.
- Plan show, try and discuss, with timings.
- List materials so everyone can try.
- Decide how you will check each farmer can do it.
- Choose a time, place and language that suit the farmers.
Words to know:
- Show, try, discuss: a teaching method: demonstrate, let everyone practise, then talk it through.
- Lesson plan: a short written plan of what you will teach, how, with what, and how long each part takes.
- Learning by doing: learning a skill by practising it with your own hands.
Try it now: Write a lesson plan for one skill you know well: the skill in one sentence, materials, the show-try-discuss timings for 60 to 90 minutes, and how you will check that each farmer can do it.
You can now plan a short training session that teaches one skill by show, try and discuss.

check.q: Which is the best skill for one 90 minute session?
options: Planting maize in rows with a handful of compost per hole
check.why: One clear skill can be shown, practised and checked in one session.

options: The trainer gives a long talk
Every farmer does the skill while the trainer watches and helps
check.why: Practising with their own hands is how adults remember.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Demonstration plots and farmer field schools
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Lay out a demonstration plot that fairly compares the usual practice with a new one.
This lesson builds toward: For a practice you want farmers to adopt, you will lay out a demonstration plot that compares the usual practice with the new practice, with plots of the same size, labelled, recorded and visited on set dates.
Farmers believe what they see on a farm like theirs. A demonstration plot shows a new practice side by side with the usual one. Choose a visible place near a path, with even soil. Mark two plots of the same size (for example 10 m x 10 m each): plot A, the usual practice; plot B, the new practice. Change only one thing between them, such as the variety, spacing or compost, so the difference has one cause. Put a clear sign on each.
Keep records from the start: planting date, inputs and labour for each plot, photos every two weeks, problems, and the harvest weighed separately. Plan field days at key stages (after emergence, at flowering, at harvest) so farmers can see and compare. Be honest if the new practice does not win: that is useful learning too.
A Farmer Field School (FFS) goes further. FAO describes it as a group of farmers who meet regularly in a field through a whole production cycle, guided by a trained facilitator. They compare plots (local practice and a proposed better practice) and do Agro-Ecosystem Analysis: in small groups they observe plants, pests, natural enemies, soil and weather, draw what they see, and decide together what to do. FFS has been used in more than 90 countries. If you want to facilitate one, ask your extension office or a project about facilitator training.
Step by step:
- Choose a visible spot with even soil.
- Mark two plots of the same size: usual and new practice.
- Change only one thing between them; label both.
- Record dates, inputs, labour, photos and the harvest by plot.
- Plan field days at emergence, flowering and harvest.
Words to know:
- Demonstration plot: a small plot that shows a practice so farmers can see it working.
- Farmer Field School (FFS): a group that meets regularly in a field through a season, guided by a facilitator, to learn by observing and testing.
- Agro-Ecosystem Analysis (AESA): observing plants, pests, natural enemies, soil and weather in a field, then deciding together what to do.
Official sources:
- FAO Global Farmer Field School Platform: overview
Try it now: Draw a demo-plot layout for the skill you planned in Lesson 2: two plots of the same size, the one thing that differs, the signs, what you will record, and the dates of three field days.
You can now lay out a fair demonstration plot and explain how a farmer field school works.

check.q: In your demo, plot B has a new variety AND compost AND wider spacing. What is the problem?
options: You cannot tell which change made the difference
check.why: Change one thing so the difference has one cause.

check.q: What do farmers in an FAO farmer field school do in Agro-Ecosystem Analysis?
options: Observe the field in small groups and decide together what to do
check.why: AESA is observing plants, pests, soil and weather, then deciding as a group.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Advising, earning and showing results

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Reaching farmers by phone, and knowing when to refer
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Give only advice you are trained for and refer farmers to the right expert.
This lesson builds toward: When a farmer asks for advice beyond your training, you will give only advice you are trained for and refer the farmer to the right expert, using a written referral list and never giving drug doses or recommending unregistered pesticides.
Phones help you reach more farmers between visits. Record a short video (one to two minutes) of the "show" step on your phone and share it in a WhatsApp group; send reminders by SMS for farmers with basic phones; use voice notes in the local language; hold a short group call before a field day. Ask permission before you film people or their farms, and keep the group for farming topics only.
Advice can help or harm. Advise only on what you were trained for and have seen work. Never give doses for animal drugs, vaccines or hormones, and never give withdrawal periods: say "follow the vet and the product label". Recommend only pesticides registered in your country (for example with Kenya's Pest Control Products Board or Nigeria's NAFDAC), used as the label says, with protective equipment. Check the registration body's list if you are unsure.
Refer quickly when something is beyond you: sick or dying animals go to the vet; sudden deaths of pigs or poultry may be African Swine Fever or avian flu, which are notifiable, so tell the farmer to report to the vet or veterinary authority at once and not to move or sell the animals. Unknown pests or diseases on crops go to the extension office or a research institute. Loans and contracts go to a trusted adviser. Keep a written referral list with names and phone numbers, and follow up to see what happened.
Step by step:
- Share short videos, SMS reminders and voice notes; ask permission before filming.
- Advise only on what you were trained for.
- No doses or withdrawal periods: vet and label only.
- Registered pesticides only, as the label says.
- Refer quickly using your written referral list, and follow up.
Words to know:
- Referral: sending a farmer to an expert who can help with something beyond your skills.
- Notifiable disease: a disease that by law must be reported to the veterinary authority, such as African Swine Fever or avian flu.
- Registered pesticide: a product approved for use by the national regulator.
Official sources:
- Pest Control Products Board (Kenya): registered products
- NAFDAC (Nigeria): registration of agrochemicals
Try it now: Write your referral list: the nearest vet or veterinary office, the extension office, the pesticide registration body for your country, and a trusted adviser for money and contracts, with phone numbers. Then write three questions you will NOT answer yourself and who you will send them to.
You can now reach farmers by phone and give advice within your limits, referring the rest to the right expert.

check.q: A farmer asks how much antibiotic to give a sick goat. You say:
options: "Call the vet and follow the product label; I cannot give doses."
check.why: Doses come from the vet and the label, not from a farmer trainer.

check.q: Several pigs in a village die suddenly. What do you tell the farmers?
options: Report to the vet or veterinary authority at once and do not move the pigs
check.why: It may be African Swine Fever, a notifiable disease that must be reported at once.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Earning a living as a Farmer Business Advisor, ethically
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set out how you will earn from inputs and services and the ethical rules you will follow.
This lesson builds toward: If you sell inputs or services to the farmers you train, you will set out how you earn and the ethical rules you follow, with written prices, commissions disclosed and no pressure to buy.
An FBA earns by bringing inputs and services to farmers who are far from shops: commission on seed, fertilizer, hermetic storage bags or tools sold; fees for services such as spraying with proper equipment, ploughing, soil sampling, aggregating harvests for buyers, or record keeping. iDE notes that an FBA's long-term ties to the community give them a strong reason to recommend only products that pay off for farmers.
Ethics is good business. Sell only genuine, registered products from licensed suppliers. Write your prices down and tell farmers when you earn a commission. Recommend what the farmer needs, not what pays you most; say clearly when the best answer is "you do not need to buy anything". Never pressure people, never sell on credit you know they cannot repay, and keep training separate from selling: everyone can attend a training whether or not they buy.
Know your numbers. Example only: if you earn a commission of XOF 500 per bag and sell 120 bags in a season, that is XOF 60,000, before your transport and time. Keep a simple record of sales, commissions and service fees, and check if any business registration or licence is needed in your country for selling inputs, especially agrochemicals.
Step by step:
- List the inputs and services you can offer.
- Write your prices and your commission on each.
- Write your ethical rules: genuine products, disclose commissions, no pressure, training open to all.
- Record sales, commissions and fees.
- Check registration and licence rules for input dealers.
Words to know:
- Commission: money a seller earns for each item sold, paid by the supplier.
- Service fee: money charged for doing a job, such as spraying or ploughing.
- Conflict of interest: when what pays you most is not what is best for the person you advise.
Official sources:
- iDE: Farm Business Advisors
Try it now: Write a one-page FBA business note: three inputs or services you could offer, an example price and commission for each, a season's example earnings, and your five ethical rules.
You can now plan how to earn as an FBA from inputs and services while keeping farmers' trust.

check.q: Which is an ethical FBA rule?
options: Tell farmers when you earn a commission
Only train people who buy from you
Push the product with the highest commission
check.why: Disclosing commissions keeps advice honest and builds trust.

check.q: A farmer's crop does not need fertilizer this season. You should:
options: Say nothing and sell a smaller bag
Tell them honestly they do not need to buy it
check.why: Long-term trust is worth more than one sale.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping training records and planning your training day
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Keep a training register with consent and plan a full training day.
This lesson builds toward: After each training, you will record who you trained, on what, and the results, with consent, kept private, and a follow-up at least once. Given one practice you know well, you will plan a 60 to 90 minute training session that follows show, try, discuss, with one clear skill, timings, materials and a check that every farmer can do it. For a practice you want farmers to adopt, you will lay out a demonstration plot that compares the usual practice with the new practice, with plots of the same size, labelled, recorded and visited on set dates.
Records show what your work achieves, help you follow up, and are what projects, cooperatives and employers ask for. Keep a training register for every session: date, place, topic, each farmer's name, gender, age group (youth or not) and village, and a phone number only if they agree. Note whether each farmer could do the skill by the end.
Follow up at least once, for example a month later or at harvest: did they use the practice, on how much land or how many animals, and what happened? Record the demo-plot results by plot. Over time you can say, for example, "I trained 60 farmers; 35 now plant in rows; their maize yield rose on average", backed by records. Do not invent numbers: if you did not measure it, say so.
Ask permission to record people's details, explain why, and keep the register private: on paper in a safe place or a locked phone, not in a public WhatsApp group. Kenya, Nigeria and other countries have data protection laws. Now put everything together for your training day: the lesson plan, the demo plot, your referral list and this register.
Step by step:
- Make a register: date, place, topic, name, gender, age group, village, phone with consent.
- Note who could do the skill by the end.
- Follow up at least once and record what changed.
- Record demo-plot results by plot.
- Keep the register private; ask permission first.
Words to know:
- Training register: a list of who attended a training, on what, and the results.
- Follow-up: checking later whether farmers used what they learned and what happened.
- Consent: a person's permission to record or share their details.
Official sources:
- Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (Kenya)
- Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)
Try it now: Final task: plan your training day. Write the 60 to 90 minute lesson plan (show, try, discuss, with the skill, materials, timings and check), the demo-plot plan (two labelled plots of the same size, the one difference, records and field-day dates), your referral list and what you will not advise on, and a training register sheet with a consent line and a follow-up date.
You can now plan a full training day and keep records that show who you trained and what changed.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Lesson plan A talk with no practice, or several skills at once. One skill, show-try-discuss with timings and materials, fitting 60 to 90 minutes, with a check that each farmer can do it. Also plans for women and young people to attend and includes a short phone video or SMS follow-up. Demo plot No comparison, or plots differ in several ways. Two labelled plots of the same size that differ in one practice, with records and field-day dates. Includes how harvests will be weighed by plot and shared honestly, even if the new practice does not win. Safe advice and referral Gives doses or names unregistered products; no referral list. A referral list with contacts, and what the trainer will not advise on, including notifiable diseases. Names the national pesticide registration body and how to check its list. Fair earning Training tied to buying, or commissions hidden. If selling, written prices, disclosed commissions and training open to all. Includes example season earnings after costs and a rule for saying "you do not need to buy". Records and roles No register, or personal data shared openly. A register with consent, a follow-up date and private storage; the local extension contact is named. Records both demo-plot results and farmers' adoption at follow-up. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Before writing a farmer's phone number in your register, you should:
options: Ask their permission and explain why
check.why: Consent is needed to record personal details.

check.q: You did not measure yields after training. In your report you should:
check.why: Honest records are worth more than invented results.
